ADHD is a widely recognized neurodevelopmental disorder that affects children, and emerging research suggests an underlying neural basis. By combining advanced machine learning and functional neuroimaging, we are able to explore complex patterns in the brain. To address the need for large-scale ADHD datasets, our team created the N-ADHD dataset, consisting of 1000 children's and adolescents' MRI scans, and in an equal number with normal brain activity. To identify key brain regions for distinguishing between ADHD patients and healthy controls, we applied a variation of the VAE attention model. By analyzing fMRI data, we discovered that attention is crucial in separating the brain activity patterns of ADHD patients and healthy controls. The validation using an independent dataset confirmed the effectiveness of attention in classification tasks. The visual representation of attention also revealed the prefrontal cortex, cortex, and thalamus as important neural areas for detecting ADHD. These findings provide valuable insights into the underlying neural basis of ADHD and suggest that identifying these key regions can lead to more accurate diagnoses.

Over recent decades, graph theory-based modeling of contagion spread has been effective in simulated scenarios.  However, existing models primarily assume a uniform time frame for disease transmission, which does not accurately reflect the complexities of the contagion process.  In reality, the time it takes for diseases to spread varies significantly, particularly between infectious and infectious periods, with some diseases like influenza exhibiting short incubation and infectious periods, while others like HIV have much longer ones.  To address this limitation, we introduce an SISI model that accounts for varying infection timeframes, utilizing stochastic processes to simulate disease transmission.  Our novel model estimates the probability of infection based on the distance between infected and susceptible nodes, as measured by the shortest path between them in a graph, and further refines this probability estimate by accounting for the length of the shortest path.  We demonstrate the efficacy of our new model by comparing simulations of the SISI and traditional SISI models against empirical data for global influenza outbreaks, our laboratory's custom dataset featuring customized agent characteristics, and datasets representing the spread of computer viruses.  Our SISI model with time-dependent infectious and incubation periods provides a more accurate representation of the contagion process, making it applicable to the analysis of various diseases.

A newly developed artificial intelligence system, named MadDog, utilizes advanced neural networks to identify and clarify the meanings of abbreviations used in technical documents. The system's capabilities have been tested using a specially created dataset consisting of numerous acronym instances accompanied by corresponding annotations, and its performance has shown significant advancements compared to existing methods. Moreover, a publicly accessible web interface for MadDog is provided, featuring a user-friendly interface for interaction and a set of tools to enhance the accuracy of the model, including a knowledge graph that contains extensive terminology and acronym knowledge.

Heat and electric currents flow through a complex setup called a mesoscopic electric heat engine, passing through a quantum Hall material that has been split into two parts by a specially designed barrier. The two parts are cooled at opposite ends and connected to additional non-interacting quantum Hall material that's kept at the same temperature difference. The first part's unique property allows its temperature to be controlled in a way that perfectly matches its own intrinsic behavior, thanks to interactions within it that cause electrons to switch their direction of flow. The two parts' simplified behavior causes them to always conduct heat in the same direction, thanks to a simple relationship between heat and electricity. The key to making the setup work lies in the unique properties that can be controlled in the more complex section, allowing the experiment to both reverse the direction of heat flow and maximize its magnitude.

Ensuring data durability, efficient management, and quick retrieval in DNA-based storage systems relies on a organized hierarchical structure of the encoded information.
This needs regular updates, which in our current methods are costly due to the high expense of synthesis.
To address this issue, we've developed a new approach that utilizes a well-structured hierarchy within the encoded information to allow for manageable updates, at a much lower expense.
Our solution enables the replacement of a relatively small section of the encoded information while preserving the overall hierarchy, which in turn, facilitates the quick decoding of all stored data through minimal new synthesis.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed hierarchy using a based-Berlekamp-Meshulam (BBM) polynomial-based framework, which also provides the required error correction capabilities.
Our proposed method achieves a synthesis cost efficiency of a factor of M (the number of documents stored), which when combined with the efficient management costs of existing methods, results in significant overall expense reductions.

The concept of band topology has evolved rapidly over the last 20 years, 
    driven by the analysis of wave function characteristics in both real and 
    momentum space. While momentum space nodal points and lines have been 
    extensively researched, momentum space nodal surfaces have only recently 
    gained attention following the discovery of zero energy surface in the 
    photonic example by Schindler et al. (2020). This review delves into the 
    theoretical underpinnings of nodal surfaces and outlines recent 
    implementations in various materials and synthetic systems.

The primary goal of this research was to determine how pacemaker-generated wave propagation speed is influenced in a one-dimensional excitable system with a spatially changing threshold for excitation. Following the initial findings by Coombes and Bressloff in 1999, a comprehensive mathematical model for pacemaker dynamics was developed. This led to the creation of approximate equations describing pacemaker voltage changes. However, these models often assume a uniform environment, which isn't always the case. This research focused on understanding pacemaker dynamics in the presence of spatial spatially inhomogeneous thresholds. Two methods were used to analyze this: a speed determination method developed by Coombes in 1999 and the asymptotic speed calculation for large times in Bressloff's model. While these methods provided valuable insights, they weren't entirely accurate in all scenarios. This research provided further analytical estimates for pacemaker generation speeds in a specific spatial profile of the threshold. Following the estimates, a verification process using numerical simulations confirmed the accuracy of these estimates.

A new, comprehensive approach is proposed for estimating a quantum system's density matrix with guaranteed accuracy in the trace norm, utilizing a sample complexity of $\tilde O(\kappa\Delta\lambda d^{O(\log d / \log \log d)}\epsilon^{-2})$. It's also determined that for a specific class of functions $\lambda$, the estimated density matrix's entropy is within $\tilde O(\log d/\epsilon)$ of the true entropy, leading to the conclusion of min-max optimality. Additionally, it's found that when $\rho$ is unitary invariant, the sample complexity is reduced to $\tilde O(d/\epsilon^2)$. This results in the development of two novel algorithms for estimating a quantum system's von Neumann entropy - a method that can estimate the entropy to additive multiplicative error with a sample complexity of $\tilde O(\kappa\lambda b\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$, and another algorithm for achieving a multiplicative error of with a sample complexity of $\tilde O(\kappa\lambda b\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$. These new algorithms outperform existing methods in terms of both sample complexity and multiplicative error. Furthermore, it's found that when a quantum system's density matrix has low entropy $h$, the updated method is efficient with a sample complexity of $\tilde O(\kappa\lambda b h \epsilon^{-2})$. The substantial data amassed by enterprises over the years serves as the cornerstone for developing sophisticated Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, albeit often hindered by technical limitations. The primary obstacle lies in efficiently utilizing this data, specifically through effective data storage and optimization in conjunction with the proper selection of hardware. To overcome these challenges, this research focuses on the essential AI technical components, encompassing data retention strategies, optimal hardware utilization via both on-premise servers and cloud infrastructure, as well as the design of an AI pipeline that integrates the entire AI solution end-to-end. The study also includes an analysis of the financial implications and pricing structures tied to each technical aspect, as illustrated through real-world case studies.

Recent advancements in deep learning have made significant contributions to Natural Language Processing, with a notable increase in NLP's ability to perform automated text classification tasks without requiring extensive supervision. This advancement is particularly beneficial in the diagnosis field, where structured diagnoses are automatically extracted from unstructured clinical notes as ICD codes. This paper outlines a novel and efficient method for ICD code extraction using a combination of BERT and a Random Forest classifier, demonstrating improved accuracy in identifying diagnoses. The proposed approach outperforms conventional rule-based methods by 10.3% and a previous supervised method using BiLSTM-CRF, with results validated through experiments using the MIMIC-III database.

Consider a monomial ideal $I$ in a polynomial ring $S$, where it is nearly Cohen-Macaulay with a height of $r$, and has a linear Betti number at degree $r+1$. We demonstrate that the colon ideal $(I:x)$ can only be generated by a set of $r$ variables whose product is not within $I$, given that $I$ meets the perfect condition. Additionally, we establish that a nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideal $I$ satisfies the strong Serre condition if and only if it is Cohen-Macaulay.

Recent advancements in quantum technology have led to the creation of increasingly complex quantum systems, which in turn has enabled the potential for quantum machine learning. However, the unmonitored learning of large-scale quantum data requires substantial processing power, presenting a major challenge to current quantum devices. A novel approach to overcome this limitation involves using supervised learning guidance. In this research, we present and experimentally demonstrate a new quantum model that incorporates supervision for classifying 4-qubit data sets, specifically 2-qubit XOR data. The experiment was conducted using a superconducting quantum processor with and without supervision, showing that our method effectively leverages available quantum hardware. Furthermore, we found that the supervised learning model achieved better results on the testing data set, matching the performance of classical classifiers, which is a significant step towards scalable quantum-based classification.

The Largest Optical Transient Survey, known as KMTAnomalySearch (KAT), utilizes KMTNet to detect celestial anomalies. KAT is committed to conducting a comprehensive search across the entire sky for all forms of anomalies. To date, we have thoroughly examined 15% of the sky each season, covering 3000 square degrees. KAT has observed the 2018 prime-field observations from the first three Southern sites, encompassing 270 prime-field hours. By applying our specially designed automated algorithm to these observations, we were able to identify 107 anomalies, comprising 74 false positives and 33 unique anomalies. These new discoveries include three anomalies with M > 15, one anomaly exhibiting a large proper motion, and another displaying a distinctive red color. The data we have gathered so far serves as a foundation for our ongoing full sky search across all four quadrants.

Light transport properties are employed in various fields, such as computer vision and graphics, to derive valuable information from shadows. Historically, computer vision approaches have utilized static shadow models, whereas modern methods in computer vision and image editing have relied on direct illumination only, neglecting geometric shadow models due to their intricate calculation. Our approach presents a dynamic, form-based shadow estimator capable of learning shadow patterns and using them for direct and indirect lighting predictions. The approach's effectiveness has been validated for surface normal estimation, height map reconstruction, shape from shadow analysis, and retopology, demonstrating its potential for efficient and accurate reconstruction of 3D structures from 2D images.

Probabilistic origin-destination demand models are increasingly utilized in transportation systems, with reasoning methods often originating from theoretical assumptions about demand distributions, ignoring actual data. Our approach derives the probabilistic OD demand distribution directly from traffic count data, without prior assumptions, by first deriving the EB models from maximum entropy principles and then obtaining the OD demand distribution via Legendre transforms, aligning with existing empirical models while respecting real data constraints. Our empirical results show the models derived from data outperform traditional statistical models, with a better fit to real traffic data and reduced numerical issues, including singularities and non-physical outcomes. Furthermore, these models can be numerically computed even when demand is close to the observed traffic.

The behavior of multiple oscillators interacting together exhibits rich and varied dynamics across different systems in nature. This is primarily due to the many diverse types of oscillators that exist and their different ways of synchronizing. In order to better understand the relationship between an oscillator's characteristics and its potential to synchronize, we examined the synchronization patterns in diverse arrays of identical and non-identical oscillators, all characterized by the same dimensionality. The results obtained for both homogeneous and heterogeneous oscillators were then compared, revealing that the synchronization behavior in diverse arrays can be predicted by a simple index that is based on the oscillator's complexity and the level of disorder in its parameters. This new measure, which is analogous to those used in diverse systems of zero-dimensional units, also provides insight into the organization of the global system's behavior. Additionally, the results indicate that the most effective type of connection for promoting synchronization is one that is local in nature and includes some irregularities in how the oscillators are connected to each other.

Two well-known algorithms for uniformly spanning tree generation on finite graphs - the Aldous-Broder and Wilson methods - rely on random walks. However, in a surprising twist, it has been observed that in a uniform spanning tree, the edges traversed by a random walk in Aldous-Broder grow at a uniform rate, mirroring what would be expected in Wilson. This phenomenon can be exploited to devise a two-phase algorithm for uniformly spanning tree generation, such that a initial walk between two randomly selected nodes, combined with a subsequent acceptance rejection phase, yields the desired uniform tree. This approach was implemented and tested on a set of uniform graphs, including hypercubes and complete graphs.

Multiple datasets have been developed to advance research in multimedia information retrieval by focusing on two tasks: either using music and text together, or using music and audio together. However, these datasets cannot be used for two tasks simultaneously, limiting their overall utility. To address this limitation, a new dataset called MusicTM has been created, combining music scores, lyrics, and audio to support two applications: simultaneous use of music scores, lyrics, and audio. The underlying assumption is that music scores, lyrics, and audio share inherent similarities. The MusicTM dataset can facilitate research into unified multimodal representation learning.

A recent breakthrough in Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been the rise of
distributed semantic models, which effectively capture and encode linguistic data.
This has also led to the integration of word embeddings in mixed media systems,
where they are combined with other forms of media, such as images, for more
comprehensive data analysis. In our research, we have successfully integrated
word embeddings with a custom knowledge graph that uses Semantic Web technologies,
namely Ontodia and Wikidata. This setup allows us to utilize the strengths of both
knowledge graphs and word embeddings for more efficient data exploration.

The impact of intensity-sensitive dispersion on soliton behavior in dark soliton-bearing optical systems was investigated through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, primarily focusing on the Schrodinger equation with an adjustable dispersion coefficient. This equation accounts for self-focusing nonlinearity and boundary conditions representing a optical beam array. Our findings demonstrate that intense dark solitons can trigger a transition from anomalous to normal dispersion, yielding periodic wave patterns. However, weak dark solitons remain stable even in situations where they induce a shift towards the anomalous dispersion regime. To gain insight into soliton behavior, we employed both analytical methods and numerical solutions, solving the governing equations using perturbation theory. Moreover, we analyzed the soliton profiles through a homogeneous transformation. Our research reveals that dark solitons can exist in various dispersion conditions, particularly in systems like the femtosecond Kerr lens mode-locked Ti:sapphire laser, and potentially offer new approaches for generating such solitons.

In visual analytics, large datasets are examined by integrating human insights.
The various methods used to explore data can result in an overwhelming number of options, leading to a lack of structured guidance for meaningful analysis.
We introduce a new and organized framework for supporting analytical exploration, referred to as a Lotse.
A Lotse embodies a specific perspective on exploring data, composed of distinct, contextually related views that together provide structured guidance for our understanding.
We present three practical examples of Lotses based on real-world data sets, which demonstrate their effectiveness and versatility in addressing different exploration objectives.
These examples also illustrate the adaptability of Lotses to support ongoing investigation.
Ultimately, we envision Lotses as a foundational concept for the future of visual exploration methods.

Numerous strategies exist for creating magnetic fields in a tokamak, each offering distinct advantages. The stellarator magnetic field's complexity necessitates advanced computational modeling and state-of-the-art 3D manufacturing techniques for the magnet system. Recent research focuses on developing stellarators with optimized coil configurations to accommodate various operating points, thereby enhancing performance in multiple scenarios. Following a similar approach, various magnetic topologies on various grid sizes were analyzed, and the optimal configuration of limited coils was determined, enabling a wide range of magnetic configurations with enhanced performance. Notably, these new designs also have the potential to support alternative topologies such as nested reverse shear and double nested shear.

A new technique has been developed to rapidly visualize temperature changes in a bed of particles using a method called MRI. By utilizing a specially designed probe with a temperature-sensitive contrast agent, we were able to map out the thermal distribution within a test container of 10 by 15 by 200 cm in size. The experimental setup involved checking the thermal patterns within a bed of solid particles while they were being fed into the test container in one end and removed in the opposite end in a horizontal orientation. A numerical model was created to simulate the thermal patterns in a similar setup, incorporating particle interactions and fixed boundaries. By comparing the results of the MRI scans with those of the numerical model, we found excellent agreement in several key parameters. This research demonstrates the feasibility of using MRI as a non-invasive tool to study particle interactions in the field of fluidization engineering.

Recent research has highlighted the importance of liquid-liquid phase separation in forming cellular condensates, with growing evidence suggesting a role in both normal cell function and the development of cell misbehaviors. To further understand the principles underpinning phase separation, we set out to explore the effects on phase separation behavior when multiple proteins, individually capable of phase separation, interact in a mixture. Using a simplified model, we found that protein mixtures exhibit unique phase separation characteristics, distinct from those of the individual proteins. Specifically, we observed the emergence of retrograde critical temperatures and the potential for sustained liquid droplet formation. Additionally, we identified conditions that could lead to the complete dissolution of droplets in certain protein mixtures. These results align with observations in condensates containing FUS and GCN5, prompting us to explore the general implications for cells. We concluded that the behavior of protein mixtures in cells may be more complex than previously thought, with the critical temperature potentially not the only factor governing phase separation.

This study examines the dynamics of a major sunspot group (NOAA AR 11429) through the analysis of H-alpha images, vector magnetograms, and X-ray flare data. It's discovered that the sunspot group underwent a rotational motion, causing one component to shift from the central to a western latitude of the active region. This region experienced two significant solar flares (M1.4 and M5.1) within a 48-hour timeframe. It's observed that the H-alpha images reveal two key areas where the plasma is heated and where the vector magnetograms indicate a disruption in magnetic field structure. These disturbances coincide with the M5.1 flare. It's also observed that the H-alpha images show disturbances in the other key area at the time of the M1.4 flare. This study confirms that the rotation of sunspot groups is crucial for the generation of significant solar flares within such groups.

The b principle, a fundamental concept in algebraic geometry, asserts that a generic complete intersection variety has a specific property: its general hyperplane section fails to interact with non-compactible rational paths. Building upon a previous demonstration of the b principle's validity for certain varieties, we expand its applications to include a broader category of "almost complete" intersections in space. Verifying these results requires an in-depth examination of singular points on specific, highly curved surfaces. Our findings also provide positive answers to two long-standing conjectures related to the geometry of these surfaces.

A reliable cardiac simulator depends on accurate numerical models, which is where cardiac mechanics comes in. Mechanically modeling the heart is complicated due to its varying properties, leading to problems with matrix conditioning. This is where scalable multilevel solvers, specifically ALBMC, come in. This study compares the Multigrid Linear Block Factorization Multigrid Conditioner method to other advanced solvers. Our research demonstrates that an innovative linear block factorization approach can achieve a robust and efficient solver, comparable to more traditional methods like HAMM, but with greater scalability.

The analysis of evolving interest areas in user-generated tagging systems reveals the dynamic nature of online tagging systems. It is possible to gain insights into emerging user interests by examining tag usage trends over time, which also reflects areas of user collaboration and resource sharing. A study on Flickr's evolving user interest landscape from 2004 to 2014 identified several recurring patterns of user engagement, including initial bursts of activity followed by periods of steady growth, often accompanied by the creation of structured tagging schemas. Tagging systems exhibiting stable long-term growth rates allow users to maintain a common vocabulary and successfully collaborate on projects, whereas those showing periodic fluctuations in user interest often indicate the renewal of user engagement in specific areas, such as the launch of related initiatives. Areas of collaborative tagging characterized by high levels of user contribution and structured schemas are associated with enhanced collaboration and resource reusability.

Recently developed acoustic metamaterials have the potential to control and manipulate long-wavelength sound waves. By designing microstructures with specific properties, these materials can control sound waves with a feature size as low as 10 times the wavelength. This research presents a high-performance, thin metagrating acoustic device constructed from microscopic resonators made of a specialized material, two-photon polymer. Using computer-designed patterns, arrays of resonators were fabricated in a layer only 50 micrometers thick, effectively operating at its first resonant frequency of 41.5 megahertz. By analyzing the transmission properties of the metagrating, researchers discovered that sound can be significantly blocked or transmitted above the design frequency, with blocked sound being redirected as a new plane wave at an altered angle. Additionally, sound may be generated at multiple frequencies as it propagates at different angles. The metagrating's design can be customized to control and manipulate sound over a wide frequency range, from an operating frequency of 41.5 megahertz down to a wavelength of 7.1 millimeters, making it an ideal platform for developing advanced acoustic devices.

This research examines the extensive time behavior of robust solutions over the entire plane for a two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model involving non-isothermal phases. By analyzing the Fourier transform in space and employing an energy inequality, we establish the existence of a globally defined, continuously differentiable solution trajectory in the exponential weighted H^3_x L^2_ω for the compressible FENE dumbbell model.

Integrating Integrated Access and Backhaul in 5G and beyond networks via wireless backhaul offers a more efficient and adaptable approach to building integrated networks. By transmitting control and data signals via wireless means, this methodology reduces infrastructure requirements and enables easier deployment. However, due to limited backhaul link range and signal range overlap, implementing IAB poses challenges in 5G and beyond integrated networks. This work provides a comprehensive overview of IAB-related challenges and potential solutions. A summary of relevant studies on integrating backhaul in integrated networks is also presented.

In evolutionary and genetic algorithms, effective performance heavily relies on appropriate parameter settings. A large number of these parameters, each with its own impact, exist in practice. A recent approach treats these parameters as variables in a mathematical function, aiming to identify the most effective combination that also considers how sensitive the function is to changes in each parameter. This research employs such combinations on various benchmark optimization problems to compare the results with standard optimization methods. The studies utilize two methods for sensitivity analysis, either considering the simultaneous effect of all parameters or individually, using two different techniques: the Sobol method and the Fast ANOVA method. A key finding is the significant influence of population size on ranking success, alongside the importance of mutation and crossover rates on solution quality.

The paper examines key controversies surrounding the application of the wave equation in quantum science, focusing on its relevance. First-order systems are typically assumed to be analogous to second-order systems; in consequence, the continuous transformation matrix is established and the first-order system's representation matrix is described. The adoption of Hilbert space and the state vector in second-order systems leads to anomalies, specifically unbounded growth in the norm of the state vector when dealing with damped waves. Similarly, forcing terms in the wave equation are represented by complex amplitudes; however, this approach is flawed as it fails to capture the continuous evolution of the state vector. The paper also highlights second-order wave equations in coupling systems, specifically crystal diffraction, raising concerns about the state vector's normal form and anomalies in the crystal diffraction process.

Despite notable achievements in reinforcement learning, numerous problems remain to be achieved, and numerous barriers hinder progress. To help navigate this complex landscape, a new platform called L2Explorer has been developed. Based on concepts from continual learning and life-longReinforcement learning, this platform provides a comprehensive collection of challenges in multiple domains, allowing for thorough evaluation. Its integrated tools and diverse tasks make it suitable for rigorous problem-solving evaluations in this area.

The Large Integral Field at a Extremely large Telescope (LIGER) prototype is a small-volume device composed of a light-collecting bucket and a custom-designed diffraction plane, utilizing a snapshot-based approach to create two spatially and spectrally resolved dimensions. Currently developed at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory, LIGER is being tested at the Victor M. Blanco Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-Observatory by taking spectra through a custom-designed scientific camera. Although research applications have been established for LIGER, the technique has the potential to serve similar purposes with other technologies. To facilitate this, a system was designed to process spectra and link it with existing software tools, including software for image enhancement, diffraction analysis, and data management systems. The overall design of this system is based on the principle of modularity and reusability and employs a method known as microservices architecture.

In the context of a 2D incompressible, inviscid flow, we've identified a scenario where smooth initial conditions can produce C^1 flow patterns that migrate towards a state of solid-body rotation. This is in stark contrast to the behavior of 3D incompressible, inviscid flows, which exhibit the same rotation effect only under specific topological constraints. Our approach relies on the precise control of the amplitude of small-scale turbulent structures, enabling the migration to solid-body rotation to prevail.

We are investigating a method that utilizes light to adjust the characteristics of a system of exciton-polariton condensates through a coupling mechanism with an optical microcavity. As a result, the optical pump creates a shift in the equilibrium position of the condensates, leading to a linear alignment effect. This phenomenon arises from the coupling between light and matter in exciton-polaritons, which are chiral in nature, and is influenced by an external magnetic field. Our computational and experimental studies show that the optical pump's orientation can be adjusted to produce various alignments within a two-dimensional plane, along with the ability to control the distance between the condensates in one dimension. Furthermore, we are exploring the potential applications of this alignment effect for creating and manipulating topological photon modes and all-optical linear logic gates based on this photon alignment.

This study draws deterministic nonlocal dynamics from a stochastic equation previously analyzed by Feng and Tsai in arXiv:2201:01593. The authors' mathematical framework includes a singular nonlocal operator analogous to a "slope-dependent term" in stochastic kinetic equations. This kinetic equation can be seen as an extension of a one-dimensional fully-convex Hamilton-Jacobi equation with random obstacles. By applying a deterministic limit, the researchers established a link between this equation and a one-dimensional nonlocal kinetic equation. The equation can also be seen as an extension of a one-dimensional fully-convex Hamilton-Jacobi equation with nonlocal constraints. The authors also discuss connections to one- and two-dimensional versions of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isakov equations.

During a COVID-19 pandemic, gathering up-to-date information about public health is crucial for local officials to make well-informed decisions. With the outbreak spreading globally in March 2020, the South African government faced a pressing need to implement effective countermeasures. In the absence of direct data collection, local health authorities in Johannesburg began using a workaround by analyzing Twitter posts in search of clues about emerging health concerns. Although this approach faced initial challenges, it eventually led to a reliable system that could track the association between COVID-19 related hashtags and actual case numbers, ultimately revealing a predictive link that allowed officials to anticipate a surge in cases a week in advance.

A crucial step in K. F. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem involved initial cases where a set had a small number of triples. This instance was initially handled by I. Z. Richman in collaboration with Freiman. Here, a refinement of Freiman's proof is presented, making use of a recent result from the area of geometry, specifically related to the concept of Helly numbers, which was recently established by J. Pach and A. Tsukerman.

A study was conducted to train a deep learning model on retinal images to detect early signs of glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy. The research focused on analyzing the retina to detect glaucoma, a condition characterized by the glial crescent, which is a sign of glaucoma. A method was proposed that combines the features of the retina with the characteristics of the optic disc, a circular area at the center of the eye, to detect glaucoma. The research found that integrating the features of the retina with the glaucoma indicator improved the accuracy of glaucoma detection.
